props.title: Born Yesterday

sections.content: Born Yesterday brilliantly captures post-war American cynicism through the lens of comedy. Judy Holliday's Oscar-winning performance as Billie Dawn set the template for the "dumb blonde" character while secretly subverting it - her transformation from kept woman to enlightened citizen delivers sharp commentary on political corruption and female empowerment. The film shares DNA with other smart social comedies of the era like Adam's Rib (1949) and The Lady Eve (1941), using romantic comedy frameworks to explore power dynamics and class warfare in post-war Washington.

sections.content: Director George Cukor, already famous for The Philadelphia Story (1940) and Gaslight (1944), brings his signature touch for sophisticated comedy while letting Holliday recreate her stage triumph. The film's exploration of corruption and politics feels especially relevant today, connecting to later political comedies like Mr. Smith Goes to Washington (1939) and Dave (1993). William Holden's patient journalist Paul Verrall provides the perfect foil for Holliday's Billie, their chemistry driving home the film's message about education and empowerment. SUBHEAD: Comedy with a Conscience

The film's genius lies in how it uses comedy to deliver serious messages about democracy and civic responsibility. Like His Girl Friday (1940) and State of the Union (1948), it tackles political corruption through witty dialogue and romantic entanglements. Broderick Crawford's Harry Brock represents the worst of American capitalism - a bullying junkman turned tycoon trying to buy political influence. His eventual downfall through Billie's awakening satisfaction carries the film's core message about educated citizenship being the best defense against corruption.
